planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade on a strong trellis or pergola; Issai is unusual among kiwiberries for being self-fertile, so a single vine can fruit without a separate male pollinator.

directions: Plant on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Issai is a self-fertile hardy kiwiberry cultivar, a rare trait among Actinidia arguta selections that are normally dioecious and need a separate male vine for pollination. This makes Issai a practical choice for a small garden with room for only one vine, though yields still improve somewhat with a male pollinator nearby if space allows. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten skin and all, with sweet green flesh and classic kiwi flavor, ripening in late summer to early fall. Issai also tends to fruit at a younger age than many hardy kiwi selections, often within two to three years of planting rather than the longer wait typical of the species. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous, twining growth and keep fruiting wood renewed, and provide a sturdy support structure from the start, since mature vines become heavy.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Kiwiberry Production Guide

planting.note: Plant male and female vines in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade on a strong trellis; Anna is a productive female cultivar that needs a male Actinidia arguta pollinator planted nearby for fruit set.

directions: Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator (one male per 6-8 females) on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Anna is a widely grown, reliably productive hardy kiwiberry cultivar valued for good vigor and heavy fruit set once a compatible male is nearby. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten whole without peeling, with sweet, bright green flesh and classic kiwi flavor, ripening in late summer to early fall. As with all kiwiberry vines, plants take a few years to reach full bearing size but then produce heavily and reliably for decades. Prune hard each winter on a permanent framework of cordons to control the very vigorous twining growth and keep the fruiting wood renewed and productive, and install a sturdy trellis or pergola from the start, since mature vines and their fruit load become quite heavy.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Kiwiberry Production Guide
University of Minnesota Extension — Hardy Kiwi

planting.note: Plant female vines with a compatible male Actinidia arguta pollinator in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade on a strong trellis; Ken's Red is a New Zealand-bred selection known for its distinctive red-blushed skin.

directions: Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Ken's Red is a New Zealand-bred hardy kiwiberry cultivar notable for its smooth skin blushed red-purple over green, distinguishing it visually from the plain green skin of most kiwiberry cultivars, with sweet green flesh and rich kiwi flavor inside. Fruit ripens in late summer to early fall and is eaten whole without peeling, like other kiwiberries. As with all Actinidia arguta selections, plants need a few years to reach full bearing size but then crop heavily and reliably for many years once established. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous twining growth, train onto a permanent trellis or pergola from planting, and keep a compatible male vine within range for consistent pollination and fruit set.

planting.note: Plant female vines with a compatible male Actinidia arguta pollinator in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade on a strong trellis; Geneva was selected at Cornell's Geneva, New York research station for reliable fruit quality and cold hardiness.

directions: Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Geneva is a hardy kiwiberry cultivar selected at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station, part of a long-running kiwiberry breeding and evaluation program aimed at improving fruit size, flavor, and reliability for cold-climate growers. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten whole without peeling, with sweet green flesh and good classic kiwi flavor. As a university-trialed selection, Geneva offers more consistency in fruit quality and vine performance than many seedling-grown kiwiberry vines sold without named cultivar status. Prune hard each winter on a permanent cordon framework to control the vigorous twining growth, provide sturdy trellising from planting, and keep a compatible male vine within pollinating range for good fruit set.

planting.note: Plant female vines with a compatible male Actinidia arguta pollinator in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade on a strong trellis; Meader was bred at the University of New Hampshire for cold hardiness and early ripening.

directions: Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Meader is a hardy kiwiberry cultivar bred at the University of New Hampshire and named for horticulturist Elwyn Meader, selected for exceptional cold hardiness and a shorter growing season requirement that lets it ripen fruit reliably even in northern New England summers. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten whole without peeling, with sweet green flesh and good kiwi flavor, ripening earlier in the season than many other kiwiberry selections. This early ripening and strong cold tolerance make Meader a dependable choice anywhere the growing season is on the short side for other hardy kiwi cultivars. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous twining growth, train onto a permanent trellis from planting, and keep a compatible male vine within pollinating range for consistent fruit set.
